results.summary: DreiMann implements a dice-based party game where two button presses simulate rolling two dice and the result is shown on a seven-segment display. The display encodes doubles as the number 1-6, a 1-and-2 combination as all segments lit, a single 3 as the three horizontal lines, and any other combination as the middle line only. It needs two push buttons on inputs 0 and 1, an optional switch on input 2 to select common anode or common cathode, and a seven-segment display wired to the eight outputs. The design is a straightforward Verilog game with no reported silicon results and is intended to be played socially rather than tested automatically.

This design is a baud-rate clock and data recovery circuit for PAM4 signals, using a Mueller-Muller phase detector, a proportional-integral loop filter, and a digitally controlled oscillator. It accepts an 8-bit data input and produces recovered sample outputs X[4:7], status bits S[0:2], and a Sample_en strobe on the outputs. The documentation consists only of the title, pin names, and a one-line description, so the exact interface timing and configuration are not explained. No test procedure, external hardware, or silicon results are given, leaving the design's operation largely inferred from the pin names.

Negative Nature #1 is a generative Voronoi pattern placed on the met4 layer as silicon artwork rather than a functional circuit. It has a single dummy output pin and no inputs, and the documentation states that it is meant only to be looked at. No external hardware is required and there is no test procedure beyond visual inspection. The project is notable as a decorative layout experiment rather than a logic design.

Lights-Out is a puzzle game implemented with a 3x3 multiplexed LED matrix and three row buttons. The design drives three LED row outputs, three column outputs, and a DONE signal, while reading three button inputs for the rows. It requires an external breakout board, for which the repository link is provided, to connect the LEDs and buttons. The documentation is brief and gives no test results or detailed gameplay description beyond the title and pin names.

Bouncing squares renders five moving squares as a screensaver-style animation on a VGA output. It uses the standard Tiny VGA pinout with two bits each for red, green, and blue plus horizontal and vertical sync, and runs from a 25.175 MHz pixel clock. The only external hardware needed is an older VGA monitor, and testing consists of plugging the board into a VGA port. The documentation is minimal, describing the design only as a screensaver with five squares.

The Brainf*ck ASIC is a hardware interpreter for the Brainf*ck language that stores its tape in external SPI RAM and communicates with a host over a two-wire serial link. It accepts encoded instruction bits and validity on its inputs, drives SPI chip select, MOSI, MISO, and clock on the bidirectional pins, and exposes transmit, interrupt, and inspection signals on the outputs. Testing requires the Tiny Tapeout I/O board with an RP2040 or RP2350 running SPI RAM emulation firmware, plus a protoboard and wiring, and programs are converted from Brainf*ck source with a provided Python script. The design is notable for offloading bracket handling to an interrupt-driven MCU collaboration and for using external memory rather than on-chip storage.

OctoPWM is an eight-channel PWM driver controlled over SPI, with each channel having a 10-bit compare threshold and a shared configurable clock divider. It accepts 16-bit SPI transactions with a write address and value, uses active-low chip select and enable pins, and outputs eight PWM signals plus a divided clock output. The design targets a 10 MHz clock, matches the Tiny Tapeout audio pinout, and needs no external hardware beyond the SPI host. The author notes it was made in one night with no prior HDL experience and that the testbench is lacking, so correct operation is hoped for rather than fully verified.
